Messages.Author: Curevei

>Based off of a poll on texas.vekn.org, What discipline(s) do think is
>the most versatile, and why?

In my mind, a versatile discipline is likely to be one that can stand on its
own in terms of not needing another discipline to make a deck work and give
options for what sort of deck to build. So, here's a list of disciplines that
would seem to fit:

Animalism
Chimerstry
Dementation
Dominate
Mytherceria
Necromancy
Obeah
Obfuscate
Obtenebration
Presence
Protean
Spiritus
Vicissitude

I see the bloodline disciplines as being a bit different, being limited by the
number of vampires able to use them. Takes me down to 10 by eliminating them.
Presence has few combat options, no stealth and no intercept. Between Protean
and Vicissitude, I'd take the latter. Obfuscate is limited in actions (among
other problems). I'd take Dominate over Dementation. Take Chimerstry over
Animalism.

Chimerstry
Dominate
Necromancy
Obtenebration
Vicissitude

Chimerstry has an interesting issue in whether the high cost of cards makes the
discipline less versatile and, then, whether being able to fairly easily work
around that with Gabrin/Path removes the issue. Regardless, I'll take it over
Necromancy due to far more combat options, greater number of useful actions,
plus bleed, etc. I think I'd give the edge to Obtenebration over Vicissitude
due primarily to Obtenebration having intercept. With more actions and more
varied combat, I'd take Chimerstry over Obtenebration. Dominate has got action
variety out the wazoo and bounce, but Chimerstry isn't short on actions, has
real stealth, faux intercept, variety of combat options.

At least if you ignore the cost of Chimerstry and possibly if you don't, it
wins my vote.

I've played an Imposing Phantasm deck more times than I play most decks. But,
I'm still iffy on the reliability of the card. Deck could have just gone with
Trapparition/Crows and been hardly any different.

If you drop Crows, the opponent is still going to want to get out of combat
and, if not possible, eats a bunch of damage. If you drop Crows and IP, any
survivability play on your opponent's part = no damage done while you are using
up additional card slots. More simply, if you don't reliably put minions down
when you play an IP, you are wasting cards and blood (if not an illusion).

If you play a small number of them, then it's a crap shoot whether it helps put
a minion down, again, unlike Crows. If you play lots, well, you end up playing
lots, which may not have been the goal.

Does however produce the only way I know of that can result in both minions
gaining blood from combat (that doesn't involve "outside" effects like Blood
Tears) when both vamps Taste, which I believe happened once when I played my
deck.

As much as I think the game has a variety of problems, as most if not all CCGs

changes?

teeth.

Howdy,

> Weather Control, pre-CE, required only tiny vampires and minimal support--a

That's the theory, yes. In practice, though, you need to have
approximately 50% of your library invested in Weather Control to do
this even vaguely reliably. Lucian's a 10-cap, so if he's full you're
going to need to drop 11 WC to down him. Assuming you've got a 7 card
hand, even if you start out looking at 7 WC, you're going to need to
draw into 4 more, which will be tricky if you only have, say, 30 in 90
cards. If you do pull it off, chances are you have very few WC left
in your hand, and it may be difficult to cycle back into them,
especially once your opponents figure out that you're in a WC drought.
And Chantry just doesn't work that well when you go to torpor on your
own turn. Everyone gets a chance to snack, and you're playing
voteless weenies.

Then there's the fact that Lucian is a 10-cap with DOM; in many decks
he would just tell Roreca to sit down (Obedience), thus wasting one of
the precious rush cards in the deck.

> WC was *really* trumpy, where Illuisons is much less so, due to cost and
> upkeep requirements.

I've heard of a couple of decks that apparently made good use of WC,
but never seen one in operation. My experience suggested that it was
pretty fragile. I sometimes managed to take down someone with
significant blood on them, but rarely more than once per game.

Of course, my deck used both WC and The Embrace, so it is doubly dead,
as is the !Tory Embrace and Majesty deck... It seems to me that with
Majesty and WC 'fixed' the Embrace fix was kind of redundant. OTOH, I
never had much incentive to use Thirds or Creation Rites previously,
and so I kind of agree with the Embrace's retool. And the Majesy
retool. But I just didn't see a real case for hosing Weather Control.
(And no, it's not completely hosed - it's still just as usable for
the old for/tha bruise bleeder.)

And I really, really can't figure out why Burst of Sunlight needed to
be mangled in the way it is now: used by a vampire, it will damage
allies; used by an ally, it will burn him?!? Another amusing
corner-case tha deck concept down the drain, why?

Still, I have to agree with the earlier poster who said that it wasn't
really the card changes that caused the big controversy in CE; it was
the ill-advised layout change.

Alex

Uhhhh, let's take a look at that logic. You _assume_ "an essential free
vampire, even without disciplines, is good." But what proof do you offer?
Logically, if you make a change in a card that obviously hurts the card, then
it's either it's less useful or the change wasn't really meaningful in the
context of how the card is used. Could be either, I suppose, depending on
the deck. But I used a bunch of different Embrace decks and none of them
were all that good. Granted, I never got around to trying them with the
stealth disciplines and in retrospect I probably should have. But it was
pretty clear to me that the weeny decks everyone *hated* were decks that
recruited weenies, not decks that embraced them to create them. Embrace
decks were too slow and (stealth not withstanding) Embraces often just
got blocked and then the deck couldn't do anything else. And once you did
spend all that time creating Embraces, you tended to just make a target
out of yourself for having so many vampires.

Anyway, the upshot is: why should The Embrace get changed, all the existing
Embrace cards become obsolesced (that is, they become yet more cards that
don't actually do what their card text says it does), and the card made less
useful if as it *was*, it wasn't overpowered to begin with? And clearly
it wasn't. That's just shooting yourself in the foot. Arguably, even the
above average "good cards" shouldn't get modified unless they're quite a
bit above average because of all the downsides to rewriting cards (causing
unnecessary confusion and annoying people). The Embrace was *not* an
above average card as it was. I place it as essentially equal to Third
Tradition, which is certainly a better card if you can use it but has a
higher use requirement.

> Is the new Embrace as good as the old Embrace? Of course not, but it is

*really* narrow now. There aren't going to be many decks that can make much

The Embrace is clearly less useful now than it was. That isn't an issue. The

The Embraced was arguably better than Third before it was changed:

-Embraced: An action to create a 2 cap vampire with a discipline. That
vampire could hunt immediately. Cost 2 blood.

-Third: An action to create a 2 cap vampire with a discipline. That vampire
can't act this turn. Cost 1 blood, or 2 blood if you want the vampire to act
next turn (instead of hunting). Acting minion needs to be a Prince/Justicar.

They were both actions and cards. A wash. Embrace cost 2 blood, made an
empty vampire, but that vamp could hunt this turn. Third costs 1 blood, made
an empty vampire that couldn't hunt this turn, so you have to pay an extra
blood so that the Third vamp can act on the next turn. All of this is a
wash. But then Third has the very significant cost of needing a
Prince/Justicar. When this was factored in, Embrace was functionally better
than Third--functionally identical but with a significantly lower cost (no
need of P/J).

Assuming that Third is a balanced card, if Embraced was effectively better
when it was supposed to be worse, it makes perfect sense that it got hacked
back.

> And clearly
> it wasn't. That's just shooting yourself in the foot.

Was Embrace a "broken" card? Unlikely, but it was better than an equivelant
card that it was supposed to be worse than (Third). Thus it was fixed to put
it in line. Very much like the Banishment-Peace of Khetemon situation.

>The Embrace was *not* an
> above average card as it was.

It may or may not have been an above average card, but it was better than
Third. If Third was "balanced", and Embrace was better, it makes sense that
it gets changed.

> I place it as essentially equal to Third
> Tradition, which is certainly a better card if you can use it but has a
> higher use requirement.

Third wasn't a better card though. Yes, Third cost 1 blood but made an empty
vampire that couldn't hunt. To maintain parity with Embraced, Third cost the
acting vampire 2 blood (the same as Embraced). Then it *also* had the very
significant P/J clause.

actions effective, not stealth, not S:CE or other combat tricks, not
enhancing bleeds, nothing. It's just a helpless little bug waiting to be

well for these purposes. And such decks would have been extremely popular.

I don't understand the arguments people construct asserting how great cards
are in the face of proven tournament history to the contrary. You can see
how useful cards were or were not just by going to Jeff Thompson's Tournament
Winning Deck archive and looking. Not to mention just hanging around this
newsgroup and seeing what people spend their time talking about. There are
some Embraced sprinkled here and there in a few of the decks. Last time
I looked, I saw one deck that had 16 of them but that was the only one that

Reasonably well is fine. But can you get anywhere in a tournament with it?

I got to tournaments, they'd fall flat on their face. People just block the
the Embrace action and all the other stuff you stick in to take advantage
of your numbers turns into garbage. There's too much intercept in
tournaments to make it work well. That's why I said in retrospect I should
have played around with stealthy Embracing strategies. I don't think they'd
have become unstoppable decks but they might held their own a lot better.

> > I think you're misinterpreting the whole scenario. Never mind Peace
> > of Khetemon; it's beside the point. Merely note that Banishment was
> > considered too powerful *in general* - and got toned down. Had that not

> because there was in existance, a card that was similar but more expensive
> to compare it to. Given the existance of the comparison, one could say "Hmm.
> Which of these cards seems appropriate?" and then change the other.

This usually only works if one of the two is overpowered or one of the two
is basically wallpaper. The exception is if you have some basic function
that's intended to be part of the game and can't be ignored (e.g. Blood
Doll) and one card does the function much better than the other or they're
very similar but one has a modest advantage over the other and no comparative
disadvantage whatsoever. Banishment hardly falls in that category. Banishment
is a pretty specialized kind of thing that needs to be roughly as useful as
the general population of cards failing which it would be termed overpowered
or underpowered by itself. So, again, never mind comparing it to Peace of
Khetemon. If it was badly balanced, you should be able to see it vs. all
the other cards. If it was OK, then Peace of Khetemon was the card that
needed changing. Same with The Embrace/Third Tradition comparison. These
cards do not live in a vacuum.

Maybe the way to demonstrate this is to point out that between the printing
of Dark Sovereigns and Ancient Hearts, Banishment existed but PoK did not.
So, you're claiming that during this period, Banishment was fine. But as
soon as Ancient Hearts came out, the printing of Peace of Khetemon implied
that Banishment required errata? Seems ludicrous to me. The *real* answer
is to print a PoK that wasn't wallpaper to begin with. (Though in fact, I
would concede Banishment was a suspiciously powerful card that isn't
hurting much for being trimmed back slightly. I don't think we'll be
seeing anyone start to use PoK on this account, however.)

Likewise, had the Third Tradition never been printed, I'd wouldn't think
you'd see any reason to reduce the power of The Embrace. So it likewise
seems ludicrous to claim that printing a new card should be the sole cause
for an old card to get changed. Just make sure there are reasonable tradeoffs
between the two before you print the new card - and make sure both are
balanced against the general population.

Fred

I still claim that. Pre CE, and currently, the cost of Third is considerably

considerably lower cost than 1 blood and a Prince for an empty vampire that
can't hunt (or 2 blood and Prince for an untapped vampire with 1 blood).
Third is more expensive than Embrace, in practice.

Embrace is cheap. When they did the same thing, Embrace did too much for
what it cost, relative to Third. Now, Embrace is still cheaper than Third,
but Embrace is less effective. This is reasonable. I accept that Embrace may
now be *too* less effective, but the logic is sound.

> Were that true, no one would bother using
> Third Tradition because The Embrace was available.

When Embrace and Third both did the same thing, Embrace was a better card to
use than Third was, in most situations. Third showed up more often, however,
as it was easier to get a hold of.

> You keep trying to
> thread your argument between mutually contradictory positions.

I don't think I do. Barring the deeply confused, crack induced paragraph
that confused us both, my position is pretty non contradictory:

-Pre CE, Third and Embrace did essentially the same thing, but Embrace was
effectively "cheaper" to play.

-Assuming that Third is balanced and useful, then it makes sense that
Embrace, which pre CE did the same thing yet was effectively cheaper, became
less effective than Third.

One could certainly argue that Third *isn't* balanced or useful, and making
Embrace less effective than Third is simply wallpapering it (which is what I
think you are mostly arguing), but for my purposes, this isn't really
relevant. I dwell in a world where Third is a balanced, useful card. This is
a given in my argument:

"Third Tradition is a balanced and useful card".

This is the basis of my entire point. I accept that some would disagree,
however. Given this basis, that Embrace did essentially the same thing for a
significantly less severe cost, it is logical that Embrace has become less
effective.

> do was what they did with Freak Drive: make it an uncommon. Probably,

> over The Embrace.

generally better than Embrace (especially if you could take advantage of the

the very similar Third, which it should not have been.

> I don't understand the arguments people construct asserting how great cards
> are in the face of proven tournament history to the contrary.

I'm not asserting that Embraced was particularly great. Never have. It was
useful. It was reasonable. It was too good, relative to the more expensive
Third, which, according to the given assumption of my argument, is a
balanced and useful card. That it was better than the more expensive Third
indicates that it should have been reduced in effectiveness. It was.

I'm not, nor have I ever been, saying that Embrace needed a functional
change due to being too good, in an overall sense. Only in a "too good
relative to Third" sense.

> Reasonably well is fine. But can you get anywhere in a tournament with it?

> That's why I said in retrospect I should
> have played around with stealthy Embracing strategies. I don't think they'd
> have become unstoppable decks but they might held their own a lot better.

No. I'm claiming that PoK was part of the comparison material that made it
evident that Banishment needed a fixing.

Assuming that PoK was at the appropriate level of power (may or may not
actually be), Banishment was clearly over that appropriate level of power.

Banishment was overpowered from the get go. It is possible that it was
necessary for PoK to be printed so that the designers could be convinced of
it.

> Likewise, had the Third Tradition never been printed, I'd wouldn't think
> you'd see any reason to reduce the power of The Embrace.

Correct.

> Just make sure there are reasonable tradeoffs
> between the two before you print the new card - and make sure both are
> balanced against the general population.

That would be nice, but it doesn't always work. Embrace was too good
*relative to Third Tradition*. If Third was at the appropriate level of
power, than Embrace should be less effective. Now it is.

Possibly too less effective, but certainly less effective.

I've been following this thread with open astonishment.

Has nobody seen weenie OBF Embrace/Night Moves/Spying Mission/Tribute?

Did that deck just not get made near you? It's not viable anymore
because the Embrace doesn't get a skill card. That's a good thing.

It was a fucking brutal deck. You HAD to mob it to stop it. You can't
block the actions with any degree of consistency -- Cloak, Lost in
Crowds, and Faceless Night (as well as the Spying Mission itself) give
far too many options. Chasing down Night Moves at 6 stealth is a task
best left to the Ravnos, who probably have the best chance of stopping
this deck with multiple Draba/ANI retainers/ANI untaps. Marked Path is
an incredibly effective card here, providing stealth that just sits
around if the vampire ever needs it -- that, oh, by the way, stacks on
Cloak and Crowds.

You'd think it would move slowly, but two 4-caps with superior Obfuscate
make it go just fine -- they can make two Embraces each, and it pretty
much rolls forward on its own from there. The crypt, of course, is the
smallest obf you can find -- don't waste time going above 4 for superior
OBF, you've got 12 skill cards in the deck and you will slowly be
putting them on your Embraces so they can Night Moves at +6 stealth.

Figure turn 2, you have a 4-cap. Turn 3, you have the other 4-cap and
one Embrace. Turn 4, you have two 4-caps, a weenie from your crypt, and
three Embraces. That's six minions. Good luck blocking them all, if
you don't blow all your intercept failing to catch the first one. And
they'll be happily making more minions as they go -- a couple hunts,
some blood from the Hunting Grounds (Nosferatu *and* Assamite *and*
Malkavian; yes, you put all three in), hey, look, 2 blood, enough for
another Embrace.

Anytime you feel like pool gain, just go ahead and Tribute. Oh, by the
way, Embraces can create their own Embraces. Miss that one? Nice. You
really think you can waste time blocking the Embrace's hunt? How about
the rescue action? Yeah, Embraces can be rescued, too. How many times
can you block a stealth deck, anyway?

Would this deck win every game? No, of course not -- you Rush it early
on and it dies. Was it omnipresent? Yes. It was played at least once
every tournament in the Southeast. I know for a fact that it was seen
frequently in Los Angeles. I'm sure others can chime in with memories
of it. I'm not surprised that Peter hasn't seen it, because Peter
would've just thumped each minion into torpor as it came out. No room
for combat defense, see.

I also know for a fact that Jeff Thompson made INCREDIBLY heavy use of
it in multiple Lasombra decks, because when you get an Obtenebration or
Dominate skill card, it makes that Power Structure deck so much easier
to run -- leave the DOM Embrace untapped to Deflect one bleed, move on
from there.

Did 3rd Tradition get played before the Embrace was changed? Almost
never. Why do you think that is? Because anything you could do with
3rd, you could do better with the Embrace, because you didn't have to
get a Prince to do it.

Anyway. My point is that it wasn't whether the Embrace was broken -- it
was clearly a change made to move the game AWAY from weenies. Big vamps
simply aren't viable in the face of 6-10 minions bleeding at +3/+6
stealth each turn.

One vampire with a Sport Bike/Mr Winthrop/Attonement will make you spend
2-3 stealth cards per Embrace, just to get them to the state where they're
tapped at 1 blood. If they fail and you want to rescue them from torpor
later, that's an additional 2 blood, and then he can get intercepted on the
hunt again. If they don't fail, you're likely burning through so many
stealth cards that you'll either jam soon or run out of library before
getting through your second prey.

That's just one possibility, in addition to other options like Rush,
Anarchist Uprising, etc.

It's a scary deck, but not any more unstoppable than many other tournament
decks.

Protean than Obfuscate (Presence use has fallen since CE, of course).

often the average capacity of the crypt is above 5, including the only deck

average crypt of 6.83). The only real Weenie Obfuscate Embrace deck in the
archive is Ben Peal's 'Wonderwall' (shows up twice), that also uses Aupex

decks.

Then they should turn to Computer Hacking before The Embrace.

Most non-DOM/PRE weenie bleed decks use it. It's a costless no-discipline
card providing an inf-discipline effect. It's 'too good, relative to'
several other cards (Social Charm, Scouting Mission, etc). A 1 blood cost
or a 4-cap-or-higher requirement would be appropriate, and it would do more
for turning the game away from weenies than any change to The Embrace.

Going back to the TWDA, there are 23 decks using Computer Hacking, most of
them with <5 average cap.

Big vamps aren't viable in the face of a lot of things (DOM weenies, POT
weenies, Brainwash decks, Malk S&B, Turbo-something-or-other, etc...)

IMO The Embrace was not among the major problems for Big Vamps, and in fact
it would help quite a few of those Big Vamps decks just as much as weenies.

Can't pull up the TWDA at the moment, so I can't check on something. But, my
recollection is that there were a couple of Palla Grande Embrace decks posted
(with maybe one being a winning deck) not long after CE.

Palla Grande, Power Structure, and other "keys off of lots of members of a
clan" strategies are the ones *least* affected by the change to The Embrace.
These decks are the niche that The Embrace fits into now. Previously, could go
in all sorts of decks that didn't mind having or needed extra vamps with only
one discipline.

I'm not bothered by the change because it turned an okay card into a
conditional card. I don't think the old Embrace was this okay card Fred and
Peter have been debating about. I think it was an exceptional card.

Nor am I bothered by curbing a nonbroken but near the top of the power curve
card under the theory that taking out the top cards only moves other cards to
the top. That theory is fine when the number of cards moved up is about the
same as the number of cards that are downgraded. Doesn't hold when downgrading
some cards makes many more playable.

What bothers me, to be more specific than I have been, is that there's an
inequity in the clans due to discipline complements and to a much lesser degree
other stuff like clan specific cards, titles, etc. and that The Embrace helped
to level the playing field by giving weaker clans options for either a weenie
horde strategy or for splashing an out of clan discipline due to The Embrace's
ability to search out the skill card. The strongest clans don't need The
Embrace to be strong. Therefore, they don't lose as much as weaker clans from
the change.

If more effort was put into rotating which clans were best, I'd be less
concerned, though it would still be useful to whoever is weakest at a certain
point to have more options. While I've seen efforts to elevate weak clans to a
viable level, haven't seen much in the way of toppling the best of the best.

As for the focus on clan which some may scoff at, it's a simple (and obvious)
way to group vampires for comparison.

The skill cards were there to be, at least partially, discarded, as the
Embraces used to allow you to get them from the ash heap. Sometimes you
would use them to give one of your inferior guys better OBF, but
realistically, you were going to have two guys with OBF in the first
place.

The Embrace card itself helped out against hand jam -- simply drop the
skill card from your hand, and you were in better shape.

It was never a problem "jamming" on Embraces. You simply played them.
If you didn't have stealth in hand (rare), then you played them with a
small, disposable minion, preferably an Embrace.

>I could see an argument for the Embrace version being more explosive, but to be
>sure, someone should do a detailed comparison of the decks.

The biggie is that Embraces cost 2 blood. In the previous example, by
the time you got up to 6 minions, it had only cost you 11 pool, it was
turn 4, and all your minions had obf (with two OBF).

If you try to do this with Effective Management, there are 15 minions
who have obf and are a 3-cap or under, but only 2 of them are 2-caps and
one solitary 1-cap. To get the same skillset of minions, it'll cost you
16 pool AND you don't have your Master slots free to drop superior
Obfuscate on the little guys, or to play Tribute to the Master. Plus,
you do actually risk contesting, though that's slight.

The Effective Management version was, well, effective. The Embrace
version is stronger, due to the diminishing pool cost of your minions
(after a certain point, it's no longer worth it to transfer guys out;
you just keep one or two ready as replacement in case you lose one or
two minions, or if you need to start accelerating again).

an expert in rush decks using this tactic, but I've seen it enough times to
know it can work.

>>But that is very much my point with The Embrace change: lots of other decks
>>that aren't a problem got screwed, and whole clans were affected.
>
>
> Some were. I liked my version of the Assamite Embrace deck, but it was
> worth it to get rid of the degenerate weenie decks the card made possible.

I think we can both agree that the main purpose of the change was probably
to prevent Embraces from creating other Embraces, so there is no more
geometrical production of minions. And even if I don't think those decks are
truly 'broken', I don't really mind seeing them go.

What I don't like is the way chosen to do it, because it affects a number of
other decks. A more subtle/precise solution could be used: for example,
making the Embrace Sterile, or making the action cost 3 blood.

Flux

As you say, though, it's only really relevant if you start from
the "clan based" point of view. Which is, sure, a reasonable
way to consider the game.

But I suspect that it's not the primary way the rules team looks
at things to decide whether they should or shouldn't be changed.
Discipline-based decks seem to me at least as common, and,
especially in the "weenie" variety, at least as "winning", as
clan-based decks. So The Embrace was probably seen as too strong
(for the cost?) in discipline-reliant decks (again probably weenie
decks) which led to the change.

cost 3 blood or something like that. It'd probably still be
playable at 3 blood, but significantly (I'd imagine) less weenie-
usable.
